findings.category: numerical/domain-correctness (float dtype erasure at JSON boundary)
findings.title: Continuous-banding trace re-match uses exact float `==` for the `=`/`==` operator, so a Float32 factor the engine banded shows status='no_match' (self-contradictory) in the trace
findings.description: enrich_banding re-derives which continuous rule fired by calling _match_continuous_rule(input_value, rule), and for the `=`/`==`/`!=`/`<>` operators that helper compares the (already JSON-jsonified) cell against float(threshold) with EXACT Python `==` (lines 303-306, applied 317-321). The cell value read from the per-node eager output has been widened from Float32 to its f64 image by _jsonify_row -> to_json_safe (e.g. Float32 0.1 -> 0.10000000149011612), while the rule threshold is parsed as a clean f64 (0.1). They are unequal, so no rule matches even though the engine (which casts both sides consistently, like the rating twin) assigned a band. The result is a factor_detail with status='no_match', rule_index=-1, is_default=False, matched_rule=None — yet selected_band/matched_band hold the real engine band. This is the banding sibling of the catalogued rating-key Float32 divergence (catalog #145-147), but at a DISTINCT location (banding continuous path, not normalise_rating_key) and not enumerated in the known catalog. It misleads the actuary-facing banding explanation and feeds _attach_banding_lineage / _banding_calculation_payload with an empty match.
findings.evidence: Ran the real enrich_banding: cfg factor {op1:'=', val1:'0.1', assignment:'LOW', default:'OTHER'}, input_row={'score': 0.10000000149011612} (the exact post-jsonify Float32 image), output_row={'band':'LOW'} (engine genuinely produced LOW). Output: status='no_match' rule_index=-1 is_default=False matched_rule=None; _match_continuous_rule(f32(0.1), =0.1)=False. Control with Float64 exact 0.1 -> status='matched'. The defect is specific to Float32 dtype erasure, not the value 0.1.
findings.recommended_fix: Make the banding trace match dtype-faithful, mirroring the recommended rating fix (catalog #147 option 1): thread the source factor column's original Polars dtype into enrich_banding and canonicalise BOTH the observed cell and the rule threshold through that dtype before comparing (e.g. pl.Series([v], dtype=pl.Float32).cast(Utf8) round-trip, or compare with a relative tolerance consistent with the rest of the module, math.isclose(rel_tol=1e-9)). Add an enrichment-agreement test for a non-integer Float32 banding factor with a continuous `=` rule asserting the trace reports 'matched', not 'no_match'.

findings.title: Same-row-count fast path accepts a positionally-aligned parent row whenever the CARRIED shared columns match, with no uniqueness guard — a reorder over rows that are duplicates on the carried key shows the wrong upstream input value
findings.description: When len(parent_df)==child_len, the fast path takes parent_df.row(child_row_idx), keeps the columns shared with the child (match_row), and accepts the row if all(_trace_values_match(candidate[c], match_row[c])) over those shared columns. The shared columns are exactly the ones that survived downstream; the parent's OTHER columns (the upstream inputs the trace will DISPLAY) are not checked. If a node reorders rows (sort/group-stable reshuffle) AND two parent rows are identical on the carried/shared columns but differ on a consumed input column, the positional row at child_row_idx ties on the shared columns yet is the wrong physical row, so the displayed upstream input (and the waterfall's value_before for that branch) is taken from a different policy. This is adjacent to catalogue #27 (which is the NO-shared-column reorder case); the NEW element is that #27's repro and fix target the empty-shared branch, whereas this fires WITH shared columns present, so #27's positional-acceptance guard discussion does not cover it. The fast path trusts equal row count + matching carried keys as proof of positional identity.
findings.evidence: Reproduced the fast-path predicate directly: parent=pl.DataFrame({'key':[1,1],'secret_input':[10.0,999.0]}); the user's clicked lineage is parent row1 (secret_input=999.0) but a downstream reorder makes child_row_idx=0; match_row={'key':1}; candidate=parent.row(0)={'key':1,'secret_input':10.0}; shared=['key']; all(_trace_values_match(1,1))=True -> fast path ACCEPTS row0, so the trace would display secret_input=10.0 instead of the correct 999.0. No len(matched)==1 / uniqueness check exists in the fast path.
findings.recommended_fix: Before accepting the positional candidate, require that the carried shared columns uniquely identify the row among parent rows (or that no OTHER parent row also matches match_row on the shared columns); when the carried key is non-unique, fall through to the value-matching path (which already records ambiguity diagnostics) instead of trusting position. At minimum, when the shared columns do not pin a unique row, emit an ambiguous_row_match diagnostic so the wrong-row risk is visible rather than silent.

findings.title: _trace_values_match compares floats with math.isclose(rel_tol=1e-9) and NO abs_tol, so any near-zero value fails to match exactly 0.0 (rel tol is meaningless at zero)
findings.description: The float comparison uses math.isclose(actual, float(expected), rel_tol=1e-9) with no abs_tol. math.isclose's relative tolerance degenerates at zero: isclose(1e-13, 0.0, rel_tol=1e-9) is False, as is isclose(1e-300, 0.0). For trace row correlation this is only reached when actual != expected already (line 99 short-circuits exact equality), and because the trace is fully in-process (both sides flow from the same jsonified DataFrame values, floats pass through to_json_safe unchanged), a genuine pair that should be equal is usually bit-identical and short-circuits. The latent hazard is the inconsistency: the module documents 'floating-point tolerance' but provides none against zero, and a future caller that compares a re-parsed/re-formatted value (e.g. a frontend-supplied cell) against a column holding ~0 would mis-classify a near-zero match as a miss, then fall to value-matching that can pick a different row. It also diverges from the value-match expression _build_value_match_expr (line 189) which uses EXACT equality for non-NaN floats, so the fast path and the value-match join can disagree on borderline floats.
findings.evidence: Verified: math.isclose(1e-13,0.0,rel_tol=1e-9)=False; math.isclose(0.0,1e-13,rel_tol=1e-9)=False; math.isclose(1e-300,0.0,rel_tol=1e-9)=False; math.isclose(0.0,0,rel_tol=1e-9)=True. By contrast _build_value_match_expr emits pl.col(column)==value (exact) for non-NaN floats, so the two comparison paths use different float semantics for the same column.
findings.recommended_fix: Add an absolute floor consistent with the engine's premium/factor scale, e.g. math.isclose(actual, float(expected), rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-12) (or a documented abs_tol), and align the value-match join (_build_value_match_expr) to the same tolerance so the fast path and the value-matching fallback agree on borderline floats near zero.

findings.category: domain-correctness (waterfall display semantics for negative-magnitude steps)
findings.title: Implied multiplicative factor is computed as value_after/value_before with no sign handling, so a step that changes the sign of the column renders a negative 'x' factor (e.g. 'x-0.5') even though the operation is conceptually additive
findings.description: _classify_contribution returns ('multiply', value_after/value_before) whenever value_before != 0, the factor is finite, and the AST hint is not 'add'. When the traced column legitimately crosses or flips sign (e.g. a margin/adjustment column going 100 -> -50, or -100 -> 100 via an additive correction with no parseable arithmetic hint), the implied factor is negative (-0.5, -1.0). The waterfall then displays a negative multiplicative factor, which is not a meaningful 'relativity' to an actuary and can read as a data error. The number still reconciles (build_waterfall re-derives delta = observed - value_before from the observed chain and _check_display_consistency reapplies prev*(value_after/value_before) == observed to ~2e-16), so this is display-only, not a wrong total — but the displayed CONTRIBUTION label is misleading for sign-changing steps, and the additive hint only rescues it when the upstream expression text is parseable as Add/Sub.
findings.evidence: classify(value_before=-100, value_after=100) -> ('multiply', -1.0); classify(100, -50) -> ('multiply', -0.5); classify(-100,-120) -> ('multiply', 1.2). Reconciliation: vb*(va/vb)==va holds to float precision, so no WaterfallReconciliationError fires and the negative factor is rendered. The fallback to additive display only triggers via _operation_hint when the expression AST top-level is Add/Sub, which is absent for many sign-flipping transforms (joins, model scores, conditional corrections).
findings.recommended_fix: When value_before and value_after have opposite signs (or value_before < 0), prefer additive (delta-only) display rather than emitting a negative implied factor, and log a 'waterfall_sign_change' note — mirroring the existing value_before==0 fallback at lines 403-412 which already chooses delta-only and logs. Keep the arithmetic value-derived so the total is unaffected.

findings.location: src/haute/_trace_waterfall.py:245-275 (_check_display_consistency) as used by build_waterfall_from_steps at 484-495
findings.title: In the production trace path the C8 display-consistency guard is a structural no-op for additive steps and can essentially never fire for multiplicative steps, so the only enforced invariant is the single final-reconciliation check
findings.description: build_waterfall_from_steps always sets each step's 'cumulative' to the observed value and derives 'value' (the display amount) from the SAME observed values: display = observed - value_before (add) or observed / value_before (multiply). _check_display_consistency then re-applies prev_cumulative (op) display and compares to observed. Because the prior step snapped cumulative to its own observed value (== this step's value_before), the additive reapply prev + (observed - value_before) == observed is an algebraic identity that holds for ANY inputs (it can never fail), and the multiplicative reapply value_before * (observed / value_before) == observed holds to ~2e-16. Thus, on the production path, the per-step C8 guard cannot catch a corrupted intermediate — it only protects the hand-authored build_waterfall(steps) public API. The real enforced invariant for traced waterfalls is the single end-of-chain reconciliation (lines 501-511). This is not a wrong number, but it means the per-step guard advertised in the module docstring as the in-builder C8 protection provides no defense-in-depth for the actual trace pipeline; a future change that lets value_before drift from the prior cumulative (e.g. if observed-snapping were ever relaxed) would silently defeat it.
findings.evidence: Trace of the data flow: value (display) is computed by _classify_contribution from (value_before, observed); cumulative is set to observed; the prior iteration set value_before = its observed (snapped). Reapply: add -> prev + (observed - prev) = observed (identity, independent of display); multiply -> prev * (observed/prev) = observed (float-exact, worst relative reapply error over 200k random multiply steps measured at 2.13e-16 << rel_tol 1e-9). So the per-step inequality |reapplied - observed| > tolerance is unreachable on the production path for any well-formed value_before == prior cumulative.
findings.recommended_fix: Either (a) document explicitly that the per-step guard is purely for the hand-authored build_waterfall API and that traced-path correctness rests on the final reconciliation, or (b) strengthen the production guard to validate against an INDEPENDENT signal (e.g. the expression-evaluated factor/delta where available, or the parsed operation magnitude) rather than the observed-derived display value, so a corrupted intermediate observed value can be caught before the final-sum check rather than only when it happens to break the end total.

findings.title: Whitelist row-locality proofs exercise each construct only in isolation on a fixed 3-column frame; compositional and dtype-specific divergences are not proven (defensive gap, not a live bug)
findings.description: The §A3 proof (test_whitelisted_construct_chunked_equals_full) and meta-test (test_every_whitelist_entry_has_a_proof_case) guarantee each whitelisted method NAME has ONE chunked==full proof, but each proof runs the construct alone on the same (i:Int64, f:Float64, s:String) frame with literal/simple args. The admission logic (_row_local_call_is_supported) admits arbitrary COMPOSITIONS and arbitrary dtypes for these methods. I independently verified (polars 1.39.2) the realistic composition/dtype variants I could construct (clip(col,col), is_between(col,col), nested when/then on columns, cast(pl.Categorical), pl.lit(list), multi-statement local frames, concat_str ignore_nulls) are all genuinely row-local, so this is NOT a live divergence. The gap is the harness would not, by construction, catch a future Polars version where one of these gains an order-dependent path, nor a dtype-specific divergence (Categorical physical encoding) because the proof frame's String column always has its distinct values appear in chunk 0.
findings.evidence: Proof generator _expr_case builds exactly 'df = source.with_columns(<fragment>)' on _frame_strategy() (only 3 columns, distinct strings 'a','b','x','' appear early). cast(pl.Categorical) is admitted (is_chunk_local_polars_code==True) but has NO Categorical proof case (expr_cast proves only cast(pl.Float64)). It is chunk-safe today ONLY because pl.using_string_cache() is True in 1.39.2 (verified: full physical codes [0,0,1,1,2,2]==chunked even when first-appearance is z|y|x across chunks).
findings.recommended_fix: Strengthen the §A3 harness so proofs cover (1) at least one Categorical/temporal/Decimal dtype per cast-bearing entry and (2) two-construct compositions, and add an explicit proof for cast(pl.Categorical) that places a value's first appearance in a non-first chunk plus a downstream sort/join on it. This pins the global-string-cache assumption so a Polars upgrade that changes Categorical encoding fails CI rather than silently mispricing a categorical-keyed rate lookup.

findings.title: cast(pl.Categorical) is admitted to the chunked path; its chunk-safety depends on the ambient global-string-cache setting, which is never asserted on the chunked path
findings.description: A POLARS node with code df = source.with_columns(pl.col('s').cast(pl.Categorical)) is admitted as MAP_ONLY. Whether per-chunk Categorical casting yields identical physical encodings (hence identical downstream behaviour for any op keying on category identity/order) depends on Polars running with a global string cache. In polars 1.39.2 pl.using_string_cache() is True by default, so it is currently safe (verified adversarially). But iter_chunked_frames never enables or asserts a string cache; it relies on the library default. If a future Polars release reverts Categorical default ordering to per-frame physical (as older Polars did) or a caller disables the cache, two chunks would assign different u32 codes to the same string and a downstream sort/group/join keyed on the categorical (or any to_physical() consumer) would silently diverge between chunked and full — a wrong number with no crash.
findings.evidence: Adversarial REPL (s=[z,z,y,y,x,x], chunk 2): values equal and physical codes [0,0,1,1,2,2] match full ONLY because pl.using_string_cache()==True. iter_chunked_frames sets no string-cache context. Downstream RATING_STEP neutralises this for join keys (casts to String via _rating_key_expr at _rating.py:583/596), but a user POLARS sort/group_by on a categorical, or any to_physical() consumer, is not neutralised.
findings.recommended_fix: Either (a) reject cast to pl.Categorical/pl.Enum in the chunk whitelist (treat like a sort-dependent op) since its physical layout is not provably chunk-local in the abstract, or (b) have the chunk runner enter pl.StringCache() for the duration of all chunk collects AND add a proof pinning categorical physical encoding across chunk boundaries. Option (a) is most conservative and matches the module's fail-loud philosophy.
